subject: computing
title: Recursion: factorial(4) — the Call Stack Grows, Then Unwinds Exit Ticket

questions.prompt: A student says A recursive call replaces the caller, so factorial(4) is finished and gone once factorial(3) starts. What is the best correction?

choices.text: The student is right - the caller ends when the callee starts

The caller is not replaced: it is suspended on the call stack, still holding its place and its pending multiplication, and it resumes exactly where it stopped when the callee returns - which is why the stack unwinds in reverse order, multiplying 1, 2, 6, 24.
The base case is factorial(4), so no frames are ever stacked

questions.misconception: A recursive call replaces the caller, so factorial(4) is finished and gone once factorial(3) starts.
questions.feedback: If you agreed with the student, that is the trap: A recursive call replaces the caller, so factorial(4) is finished and gone once factorial(3) starts. Reteach point: The caller is not replaced: it is suspended on the call stack, still holding its place and its pending multiplication, and it resumes exactly where it stopped when the callee returns - which is why the stack unwinds in reverse order, multiplying 1, 2, 6, 24.

questions.prompt: In one sentence, explain what happens to a caller while its recursive call runs.
questions.answer: The caller is suspended on the call stack, holding its place and its pending multiplication, until the callee returns.
questions.feedback: A strong answer names the call stack and the pending work: the caller waits, suspended, and resumes when the callee returns.

questions.prompt: Why does the stack unwind in reverse order?

choices.text: Because the base case returns the largest value
Because each frame can only resume when the frame above it returns, so the last call stacked is the first to finish
Because factorial(4) restarts once factorial(3) finishes
Because the frames are sorted by their return values

questions.feedback: Scene 3 shows the unwind in reverse: a frame is blocked until the call it made returns, so the deepest frame completes first and the outermost last.

questions.prompt: In one sentence, state the values produced as the stack unwinds, in order, ending with the final answer.
questions.answer: The base case returns 1, then the frames multiply in turn to give 1, 2, 6, 24, with factorial(4) returning 24 last.
questions.feedback: A strong answer gives the full chain in order - 1, 2, 6, 24 - and puts factorial(4) last, not first.
